'''''The Puzzle Palace''''' is a book written by [[James Bamford]] and published in 1982. It is the first major, popular work devoted entirely to the history and workings of the [[National Security Agency]] (NSA), a United States [[Intelligence agency|intelligence]] organization. The title refers to a nickname for the NSA, which is headquartered in [[Fort George G. Meade|Fort Meade]], [[Maryland]].<ref>The term has also been used to refer to the [[Federal Bureau of Investigation]] in the 1995 book ''The Bureau'' by Diarmuid Jeffreys.</ref> In addition to describing the role of the NSA and explaining how it was organized, the book exposed details of a massive eavesdropping operation called [[Project SHAMROCK|Operation Shamrock]]. According to security expert [[Bruce Schneier]], the book was popular within the NSA itself, as "the agency's secrecy prevents its employees from knowing much about their own history".<ref name=Schneier>{{cite web|last=Schneier|first=Bruce|title=Body of Secrets review|url=http://www.schneier.com/essay-103.html|year=2001|access-date=2012-01-17|archive-date=2012-06-18|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120618214253/http://www.schneier.com/essay-103.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Research and publication==
{{citations needed section|date=November 2021}}
[[File:William-Friedman.jpg|thumb|alt=William Friedman|The papers of the late William Friedman, who had served as the NSA's chief cryptologist, were a valuable source for Bamford. The NSA later confiscated the documents from the library at which they were held.]]

The NSA describes Bamford's research process in a partially declassified history of postwar American cryptography.<ref name=NSA-history>{{cite book |title=American Cryptology during the Cold War, 1945–1989: Book IV: Cryptologic Rebirth, 1981–1989 |year=1999 |publisher=National Security Agency |author=NSA Center for Cryptologic History |page=426 |title-link=:File:American-Cryptology-during-the-Cold-War-1945-1989-Book-IV-Cryptologic-Rebirth-1981-1989.pdf }}</ref> The history begins by describing how Bamford approached Houghton-Mifflin with a proposal to write a book on the NSA. The publisher accepted and paid Bamford a $7,500 advance.

According to the NSA's historical account, "Public Law 86-36 had served as a useful barrier against this type of research, but Bamford proved to be cleverer than others. He began with a barrage of requests for information under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA)." Bamford eventually discovered "the Mother Lode," a collection of documents deposited at the [[George C. Marshall Foundation]] Library by former NSA chief cryptologist [[William F. Friedman|William Friedman]]. These documents included copies of the ''NSA Newsletter'', addressed to "NSA Employees and their families." The account continues, "Bamford then submitted a [[Freedom of Information Act (United States)|FOIA request]] for the entire collection, using as his rationale the offending phrase indicating that the information had been intended for dissemination to uncleared people." The FOIA requests gave Bamford access to an only lightly redacted set of documents, and a former NSA employee later gave Bamford access to an almost complete collection.

During the 1975 [[Church Committee]] hearings, the [[United States Department of Justice]] (DOJ) had investigated the legal culpability of various intelligence agencies. Bamford submitted a FOIA request for resulting documents, and received most of their report on the NSA. The DOJ did not inform the NSA of the release because the investigation was ongoing, and the NSA was a possible target. The released papers were later to become the subject of threatened litigation, and their release prompted eventual rule changes that allowed for document reclassification. According to the NSA's history, "the document, with some Justice redactions, contained a good deal of information about the NSA-[[GCHQ]] [Government Communications Headquarters, a British intelligence agency] relationship, and served as the basis for Bamford's information on Second Party issues [i.e., issues regarding outside agencies with which the NSA had partnered]."  The NSA history dryly notes that "GCHQ was not amused" about the disclosure.

Bamford also interviewed retired NSA senior officials, including former director [[Marshall Carter]], with whom he talked for a day and a half. None of the discussed subject matter was classified, but, according to the NSA, "it helped Bamford to complete his mosaic." The NSA account also describes how Bamford drove through the NSA parking lot, recording [[Vehicle registration plates of the United States#Diplomatic license plates|diplomatic license plates]] and cross-checking them against known lists to determine which countries maintained representatives at Fort Meade.

The NSA's historical account summarizes Bamford's work thusly: "James Bamford broke new ground in intelligence agency research, and his techniques were adopted by others seeking to investigate reclusive federal agencies. He did it all within the limits of the law – through attributable interviews, FOIA'ed documents, and meticulous research in public libraries and newspapers. ... He 'wrote the book' on how to put together a comprehensive picture of an organization that wanted no such comprehensive picture."

==Threatened legal action and document reclassification==
Before the book's publication, the Reagan administration claimed that unclassified source documents were released to Bamford in error, and threatened him with prosecution if he did not return 250 pages of documents he had obtained through [[Freedom of Information Act (United States)|Freedom of Information Act]] (FOIA) requests. The documents in question related to a 1975-76 DOJ investigation, and described the NSA's widespread illegal monitoring of domestic communication, [[Warrantless searches in the United States|warrantless surveillance of Americans]], and monitoring of commercial cable and [[telex]] traffic.<ref name=NYT-review>{{cite news|last=Taubman|first=Philip|title=Sons of the Black Chamber|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1982/09/19/books/sons-of-the-black-chamber.html?pagewanted=all|accessdate=11 May 2012|newspaper=The New York Times|date=19 September 1982}}</ref> Bamford's attorney, believing that they would prevail in court, invited the DOJ to prosecute, but no case was ever brought.<ref name=NSA-history /> In the wake of the dispute, classification rules were revised to allow document reclassification, and the contested documents were reclassified. NSA agents then visited libraries to remove other source documents from circulation.<ref name=Forestel>{{cite book|last=Foerstel|first=Herbert N|title=Freedom of Information and the Right to Know: The Origins and Applications of the Freedom of Information Act|year=1999|publisher=Greenwood Press|location=Westport, CT|isbn=0-313-28546-2|pages=[https://archive.org/details/freedomofinforma00herb/page/115 115–116]|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/freedomofinforma00herb/page/115}}</ref><ref name=Miller>{{cite news|last=Miller|first=Judith|title=Author fights Justice's reneging on data|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=Jb4qAAAAIBAJ&sjid=HmgEAAAAIBAJ&pg=6871,7558744&dq=james+bamford&hl=en|accessdate=January 17, 2012|newspaper=Sarasota Herald-Tribune|date=15 March 1982|agency=NY Times News Service|quote=Letters from Schroeder dated Sept. 22 and Nov. 27 suggest that Bamford might be subject to federal legal action if he proceeds to publish the information as planned.}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Associated Press|title=Justice wants spy documents returned: Times|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=_SBdAAAAIBAJ&sjid=nFoNAAAAIBAJ&pg=3064,1732974&dq=james+bamford&hl=en|accessdate=17 January 2012|newspaper=St. Joseph Gazette|date=March 15, 1982|archive-date=18 May 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160518205120/https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=_SBdAAAAIBAJ&sjid=nFoNAAAAIBAJ&pg=3064,1732974&dq=james+bamford&hl=en|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Bamford |first=James |title=1984 interview |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IXwHLMckzKM |work=Charlie Rose Show |via=[[YouTube]] |access-date=2016-01-01 |archive-date=2015-12-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151229113017/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IXwHLMckzKM |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Taubman|first=Philip|title=NSA stamps SECRET on library records critical of agency actions|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=YvlLAAAAIBAJ&sjid=pu4DAAAAIBAJ&pg=7253,7285151&dq=james+bamford&hl=en|work=The Spokesman-Review|year=1983|access-date=2016-01-01|archive-date=2016-05-05|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160505205053/https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=YvlLAAAAIBAJ&sjid=pu4DAAAAIBAJ&pg=7253,7285151&dq=james+bamford&hl=en|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=Taubman>{{cite news|last=Taubman|first=Philip|title=Security agency bars access to nonsecret materials, library records show|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1983/04/28/us/security-agency-bars-access-to-nonsecret-material-library-records-show.html|newspaper=The New York Times|date=April 28, 1983|quote=While they were at Marshall library, NSA officials told the library that the visit was part of a systematic effort to track down and, if necessary, remove from circulation research materials about sensitive matters that were used in Bamford's book, library officials said.}}</ref>

The new rules allowing document reclassification were outlined in Executive Order 12356. Previously, Executive Order 12065, issued by [[Jimmy Carter]] in 1978, had prohibited document reclassification.<ref name=EO-12065>{{cite web|title=Executive Order 12065|url=https://fas.org/irp/offdocs/eo/eo-12065.htm|date=28 June 1978|quote=1-607. Classification may not be restored to documents already declassified and released to the public under this Order or prior Orders.}}</ref> Executive Order 12356, issued by [[Ronald Reagan]] in 1982, eliminated the reclassification prohibition and described situations in which documents could be reclassified. Released documents could be reclassified as long as they could be reasonably recovered (meaning that documents available to the public at large would not meet this criterion). It also allowed documents requested under the FOIA or [[Privacy Act of 1974|Privacy Act]] to be classified or reclassified provided they met specified requirements (e.g., certain matters related to national security).<ref name=EO-12356>{{cite web|title=Executive Order 12356|url=https://www.archives.gov/federal-register/codification/executive-order/12356.html|page=Section 1.6|quote=Information may be classified or reclassified after an agency has received a request for it under the Freedom of Information Act (5 U.S.C. 552) or the Privacy Act of 1974 (5 U.S.C. 552a), or the mandatory review provisions of this Order (Section 3.4) if such classification meets the requirements of this Order and is accomplished personally and on a document-by-document basis by the agency head, the deputy agency head, the senior agency official designated under Section 5.3(a)(1),2 or an official with original Top Secret classification authority.|date=2016-08-15|access-date=2017-09-16|archive-date=2021-02-15|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210215010022/https://www.archives.gov/federal-register/codification/executive-order/12356.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=FOIA-update-12356>{{cite web|last=Schroeder|first=Gerald A.|title=An Overview of Executive Order 12356|url=https://www.justice.gov/oip/foia_updates/Vol_III_3/page6.htm|work=FOIA Update|publisher=Department of Justice|accessdate=11 May 2012|quote=The new order also eliminates the prohibition against the reclassification of information previously declassified and released by providing that such information can be reclassified if it 'may reasonably be recovered.' This provision permits the Government to attempt to correct erroneous disclosures, but only where the information can be recovered from the person or persons to whom it was disclosed. Obviously, that would be impossible in the case of an erroneous disclosure to the general public. But when, for example, an erroneous release is made to a single FOIA requester, this new provision provides the Government with needed flexibility that it did not have under the previous order. This new authority, however, may only be exercised by the President and agency heads and officials designated by the President as original classification authorities. Such determinations must also be reported to the Information Security Oversight Office, which continues to have Government-wide oversight of the information security program under the new order.|archive-date=11 January 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120111023447/http://www.justice.gov/oip/foia_updates/Vol_III_3/page6.htm|url-status=live}}</ref> According to Bamford, he could not be prosecuted under the new rules because of the principle of ''[[Ex post facto law#United States|ex post facto]]''.<ref name=DN-interview-2012>{{cite news|last=Goodman|first=Amy|title=Exposed: Inside the NSA's Largest and Most Expansive Secret Domestic Spy Center in Bluffdale, Utah|url=http://www.democracynow.org/2012/3/21/exposed_inside_the_nsas_largest_and|accessdate=11 May 2012|newspaper=Democracy Now!|date=21 March 2012|quote=I was never arrested or prosecuted or anything, but I was threatened twice by the Justice Department to return documents that they said were classified. But these were documents that had been released to me by the attorney general under the Carter administration, Attorney General Civiletti. And so, I never returned the documents, because they were unclassified when they were given to me. And what the Reagan administration did was reclassify them as top secret and then order that I give them back. But we found a passage in the executive order on secrecy that said once a document has been declassified, it can’t be reclassified. So then Reagan changed the executive order to say that it could be reclassified, but that couldn’t apply to my case because of the principle of ''ex post facto''.|archive-date=10 May 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120510115736/http://www.democracynow.org/2012/3/21/exposed_inside_the_nsas_largest_and|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Reclassified source documents and American Library Association lawsuit==

Reclassified and re-sequestered source documents that Bamford had used when writing ''The Puzzle Palace'' were the subject of subsequent litigation. The NSA's historical account states that documents removed from the Marshall Library were "sequestered portions of the Friedman collection," i.e., the collection that included the copies of the ''NSA Newsletter'' that spurred one of Bamford's FOIA requests. The materials removed from circulation included three government publications and 31 pieces of Friedman's private correspondence. The [[American Library Association]] (ALA) challenged the document removal in court, and in 1987 the [[U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia]] dismissed the case. [[Ruth Bader Ginsburg]], who was at that time a Court of Appeals judge, ruled that the ALA lacked standing in the case. A lower court ruling had already affirmed that the NSA had authority to remove the reclassified documents, but criticized the NSA's "cavalier attitude" toward the classification determination of those documents.<ref name=NSA-history /><ref name=ALA-timeline>{{cite web|title=ALA Freedom to Read Foundation Timeline, 1980-1989|url=http://www.ala.org/groups/affiliates/relatedgroups/freedomtoreadfoundation/ftrfinaction/timeline/19801989/1980to1989|publisher=American Library Association|accessdate=18 May 2012|quote=Ultimately, on the appeal, U.S. Circuit Court Judge Ruth Bader Ginsburg ruled that the library associations and other plaintiffs lacked standing to bring their lawsuit in the first instance. In the proceedings below, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia had ruled that the U.S. National Security Agency had authority to withdraw the papers in question from the Virginia Military Institute library.}}</ref><ref name=Green-decision>{{cite web|last=Green|first=June L.|title=AMERICAN LIBRARY ASS'N v. FAURER, 631 F.Supp. 416 (1986)|url=http://www.leagle.com/xmlResult.aspx?xmldoc=19861047631FSupp416_1983.xml&docbase=CSLWAR2-1986-2006|accessdate=18 May 2012|quote=The Court's decision is not altered in this instance by NSA's apparent failure to comply strictly with the classification scheme authorized in Executive Order No. 12,356.4 The Court does not condone by any means NSA's cavalier attitude toward its classification determination of the materials at issue, especially the 31 pieces of correspondence. However, the Court believes that this factor alone should not be used as a means to accomplish by the back door what the Court would not permit by the front door — invalidation of NSA's classification determination and disclosure of the information in question. The threat posed to the national security is just too great.}}</ref>

==Reviews and reception==
''[[The New York Times]]'' reviewed the book favorably, writing that "Until now no one has published a comprehensive and detailed report on the agency. The quality and depth of Mr. Bamford's research are remarkable." The review concluded, "By revealing the scope and opening up the operations of the N.S.A. without giving away its most sensitive secrets, Mr. Bamford has performed an important public service in this impressive book."<ref name=NYT-review />

In a review of [[Shane Harris]]' book ''The Watchers: The Rise of America's Surveillance State'', ''New York Times'' reporter [[Eric Lichtblau]] described ''The Puzzle Palace'' as "the benchmark study of the N.S.A. [that] first pulled back the curtain to provide a glint of unwanted sunlight on the place".<ref>{{Cite news
| title = The People We Pay to Look over Our Shoulders
| date = February 22, 2010
| last = Lichtblau
| first = Eric
| newspaper = New York Times
| url = https://www.nytimes.com/2010/02/23/books/23watchers.html?ref=bookreviews
| archive-date = September 14, 2019
| access-date = February 13, 2017
| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20190914233719/https://www.nytimes.com/2010/02/23/books/23watchers.html?ref=bookreviews
| url-status = live
}}</ref> Michael Duffy, reviewing Bamford's 2004 book ''Pretext for War'', wrote in ''Time'' magazine that ''The Puzzle Palace'' "is still considered the classic account of the mysterious National Security Agency."<ref>{{cite journal|last=Duffy|first=Michael|title=One Expert's Verdict: The CIA Caved Under Pressure|url=http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,994414,00.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071012172435/http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,994414,00.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=October 12, 2007|journal=Time|date=June 14, 2004}}</ref>

''The Puzzle Palace'' has been generally well received by experts, and has been used as a textbook at the [[Defense Intelligence Agency]]'s [[National Intelligence University]].<ref name=about-author>{{cite web|title=Body of Secrets: About the Author|url=http://www.randomhouse.com/features/bamford/author.html|author=Random House, Inc.|year=2001|access-date=2012-07-03|archive-date=2012-10-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121007213518/http://www.randomhouse.com/features/bamford/author.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The NSA itself says the book "brought a new focus to the efforts of journalists and independent writers to break down the Agency's vaunted anonymity," and describes the book as "the most significant breach in NSA's anonymity since [[David Kahn (writer)|David Kahn's]] ''[[The Codebreakers]]'' in 1967."<ref name=NSA-history /> In the years between the book's publication and [[September 11 attacks]] (9/11), the relationship between Bamford and the NSA grew less adversarial. The NSA cooperated with Bamford on a later book titled ''[[Body of Secrets]]'', and in April 2001 the NSA hosted a book-signing event for Bamford at their Maryland headquarters.<ref name=about-author /> Bamford was critical of NSA actions in the years following 9/11, and the relationship between the two once again cooled.{{cn|date=November 2021}}
